newsitem.title: UK: UK parliament panel censures Conservative ex-MPs.
newsitem.headline: UK parliament panel censures Conservative ex-MPs.

text.p: A British parliamentary committee on Friday found four former Conservative MPs guilty of misconduct which it said could have merited their suspension from the House of Commons had they still been members.
But the Commons Standards and Privileges Committee said there was little it could do against the four for offences connected with payments to them for lobbying on behalf of commercial interests.
"In practice, the powers of the House to punish non-Members are limited," the committee said in a report.

The report follows Britain's May 1 election in which the Conservatives, weighed down by allegations of sleaze against several of their MPs, lost half their seats in parliament, and went into opposition for the first time since 1979.

The committee said former minister Tim Smith had accepted at least 18,000 pounds ($29,500) from Mohamed Al-Fayed, owner of upmarket London store Harrods, but had failed adequately to declare he was working for Al-Fayed in the register of MPs' interests.
"Had he still been a member, we would recommend a substantial period of suspension from the service of the House," the report said.

It recorded a similar verdict against Sir Michael Grylls, who retired after 27 years as an MP at the May 1 election, saying he had "deliberately misled" a Committee on Members' Interests about lobbying fees he had received.
Two other former MPs, Michael Brown and Sir Andrew Bowden, were less severely censured.

The committee reserved its verdict on Neil Hamilton, another former minister, who lost his parliamentary seat to an independent anti-corruption candidate in one of the most dramatic results of the general election.

Parliament's ethics commissioner Sir Gordon Downey said he had found compelling evidence that Hamilton received at least as much money from Al-Fayed as Smith and attempted to conceal his dealings with the Egyptian-born businessman.
Hamilton has challenged Downey's findings, and the committee said it had not yet examined the points he had raised.
